overview: This map label refers to medieval Croatia, including the later native kings and the kingdom’s association with Hungarian rulers from 1102. Coastal towns, monasteries and inland communities had different connections and institutions. It is a different historical entry from the modern Republic of Croatia.

periods.title: Native kings and Adriatic connections
periods.summary: Croatian kings maintained relations with coastal towns and the papacy; Zvonimir received a papally supported crown in 1075.

periods.title: A kingdom sharing a monarch
periods.summary: Coloman became king in 1102. Croatian institutions continued under rulers who also held the Hungarian crown.

sections.title: Rulers, towns and people at work

items.text: Zvonimir’s royal authority was linked to the papacy, while his marriage connected him to Hungary’s ruling family. After his death, competing claims helped reshape the kingdom. Medieval succession could turn a family relationship into a question affecting towns, nobles and armies.

Two wooden boats found in Nin’s harbor are dated to the eleventh and twelfth centuries. The surviving remains measure roughly seven and eight meters long. Their ribs and planking give physical evidence for the small craft that moved along the Adriatic coast.

The boat type known as a kondura combined rowing with square sails when winds were favorable. Oars offered another way to move when the breeze was unhelpful. Conserved remains and modern replicas help researchers explore these practical arrangements, though a replica is not the medieval boat itself.

Čika, a widow from a prominent Zadar family, founded the Benedictine convent of St Mary in 1066. Her daughters were connected with the community, and Vekenega later became abbess. Women could hold lasting responsibilities for a religious institution, its property and its records.

The Zadar convent preserved a parchment cartulary containing records from 1066 to 1236. Its writing includes Beneventan, Carolingian and Gothic forms. Across generations, the book kept track of the community’s affairs while handwriting styles changed around it.

Béla IV’s Golden Bull of 1242 granted privileges to Gradec, now part of Zagreb. The charter addressed local government, courts, taxes, markets and boundaries. A royal document could shape ordinary questions such as who judged a dispute and how a town organized trade.

The Baška tablet came from St Lucy’s church at Jurandvor on the island of Krk. Carved around 1100, it formed part of a stone screen near the altar. Its thirteen lines of Glagolitic writing preserve a record of land given to the church by King Zvonimir.

The tablet’s account names witnesses and records that Abbot Dobrovit built the church with nine brothers. This is unusually personal information preserved in a heavy piece of limestone. The stone combines a record of property with the memory of a small religious community.

The main doorway of Trogir’s Cathedral of St Lawrence carries a date of 1240 and the name of its sculptor, Radovan. The inscription also names Bishop Treguan. A signed architectural sculpture can connect a surviving building with particular people and a specific year.

Earrings with hollow metal beads survive from medieval sites including Biskupija near Knin. Gold and silver examples belong to forms used in the tenth and eleventh centuries. Jewelry records skilled metalworking and contacts with wider Mediterranean fashions, alongside the more familiar history of kings and churches.

Zagreb’s twelfth-century cathedral had three aisles and Romanesque architecture. It suffered severe destruction during the Mongol invasion of 1242, followed by rebuilding in a Gothic style. The later building therefore carries a history of damage and reconstruction within its fabric.

Latin on Radovan’s portal, 1240: “Per Raduanum”, meaning “by Radovan”. The phrase is quoted in art historian Vladimir Peter Goss’s discussion of the inscription. It preserves a medieval maker’s name in the Latin language and alphabet used for this public church inscription.

The Baška tablet includes “Zvanimir kralj hrvatskij”, meaning “Zvonimir, the Croatian king”. These are medieval Croatian words shown in Branko Fučić’s scholarly Latin-alphabet transcription. The original stone uses Glagolitic letters; this excerpt is a transcription of that script, not a reproduction of its letter shapes.

ending.text: The change of monarchy in 1102 joined Croatia and Hungary under a ruler, while Croatia retained a distinct kingdom and institutions. Medieval Croatian history continued beyond this map label’s 1279 endpoint. The later Pacta conventa text cannot be treated as a surviving original treaty from 1102.
